extracted.intended_audience: medical researchers, journal editors, and the broader clinical research community
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and arguments about requiring clinical researchers to publicly share raw/underlying data as a condition of journal publication; addresses benefits, objections, and practical precedents (e.g., NIH repository).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show your work / public availability of raw data
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should publicly share the raw/underlying clinical data that support their published findings so others can see and build on the basic facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as a fundamental scientific principle: 'show your work.' The article uses analogies (e.g., astronomers) to illustrate that withholding raw data prevents others from independently examining or building on results. Public access enables replication, secondary analyses, and scientific progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make data sharing a condition of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal editors propose that researchers would have to publicly share their clinical data in order to get their studies published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a policy proposal that could 'transform medical science' by making data availability a prerequisite for publication, thereby changing current culture of data sequestration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect patient privacy as foremost requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Patient privacy concerns must be respected when sharing clinical data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article identifies protecting patient privacy as 'first and foremost' and implies that data-sharing policies must include safeguards (de-identification, ethical/privacy protections) before public release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use established repositories / institutional mechanisms for data sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Deposit clinical trial data in recognized repositories (example: NIH repository) so others can access and reuse it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recounts depositing trial data with NIH and notes NIH maintains a repository of trials; using such repositories is presented as a practical mechanism to enable sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and welcome independent reanalysis and differing conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should accept that others may analyze the data and draw conclusions they disagree with; this is part of scientific self-correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipates objections that others might misinterpret data; counters that open access allows verification and, if a conclusion can't be supported, others can demonstrate that with the data. This is framed as a benefit, not a risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and address incentives that discourage sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that researchers may withhold data to preserve future publication opportunities or perceived control over their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains motivations (long effort invested, desire to publish additional analyses) as a real barrier and implies that policy design must account for these incentive structures if data sharing is to become common practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the anti-pattern of data sequestration or claims of exclusive understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not justify withholding data by asserting that only the original team can understand it; such claims are seen as invalid reasons to block access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author calls the claim that 'only they can understand their own data' 'inexplicable' and argues that sharing should be fostered rather than avoided; withholding on these grounds is identified as a cultural problem to be reversed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for an emotional/ownership response to sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should anticipate feeling a personal reluctance ('like my baby was being released') when releasing data and plan for that response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The speaker describes personal experience of discomfort when sharing large-trial data but notes positive outcomes afterward, suggesting policies should recognize and normalize this emotional aspect to facilitate adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterargument consideration: 'noise' vs. consensus formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Address the worry that widespread data sharing will create conflicting analyses and confusion ('add noise') instead of clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article presents the counterview that, contrary to fears, openly available data will lead to consensus as many investigators examine the same data, implying that policies should weigh these dynamics and communicate expected communal benefits.
